record.paper_title: Models, feedback control, and open problems of 3D bipedal robotic walking
record.original_question: Given an anthropomorphic bipedal robot, determine which hybrid model, including the number and nature of its discrete phases, best captures the robot's walking behavior so that stable gaits produced by the model are as human-like as possible. More concretely, identify whether there is a canonical hybrid model for studying controller development for anthropomorphic walking.

evidence.quote: This paper considered two distinct hybrid models. In the literature on bipedal robots, hybrid models have been considered with everywhere from one discrete domain or phase (which is the case for most models considered), to five.

This raises the natural question: given an anthropomorphic bipedal robot, what is the hybrid model that best captures the behavior of this system? In particular, what is the model so that when stable walking gaits are found, these gaits are as human-like as possible?
if a single “most human-like” hybrid model could be found, this could be used as the canonical model for studying controller development for obtaining anthropomorphic walking for bipedal robots.

artifact.category_tag: hybrid dynamical models for bipedal walking
artifact.self_contained_problem: A hybrid dynamical system modeling a bipedal walker consists of a finite collection of continuous-time dynamical phases (domains), each governed by a Lagrangian/ODE system on a configuration manifold subject to holonomic contact constraints, together with discrete transition maps (guards and reset maps) describing impacts and changes of contact. For an anthropomorphic bipedal robot (a planar or 3D mechanical model whose link lengths, masses, and degrees of freedom approximate those of a human), one may choose hybrid models with anywhere from a single discrete phase (e.g., a single-support phase with an instantaneous double-support impact reset) up to multiple phases (e.g., heel-strike, flat-foot, heel-lift, toe-off, and flight, giving up to five phases), each with its own continuous dynamics, guards, and reset maps.\n\nProblem. Determine, for an anthropomorphic bipedal robot, a hybrid model — specified by its number of discrete phases, the continuous dynamics on each phase, and the guard/reset structure between phases — such that periodic orbits of the closed-loop hybrid system (stable walking gaits produced by feedback controllers) are maximally human-like, in the sense of best matching empirically measured human walking data (e.g., joint trajectories, ground reaction forces, center-of-mass motion). In particular, decide whether there exists a single canonical hybrid model that should be adopted for the study of controller synthesis for anthropomorphic walking, and if so identify it; otherwise establish that no such canonical model exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of identifying a canonical hybrid model for anthropomorphic bipedal walking remains open. Subsequent literature on hybrid zero dynamics and bipedal walking (e.g., work by Ames, Grizzle, Sreenath and collaborators) continues to explore multi-domain hybrid models with varying numbers of phases without converging on a single canonical choice; no result establishing a unique "most human-like" hybrid model has been reported.

status_evidence.title: Models, feedback control, and open problems of 3D bipedal robotic walking
status_evidence.snippet: Hybrid models for bipedal robots have been considered with everywhere from one discrete domain to five; the question of which best captures anthropomorphic walking is posed as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The choice of canonical hybrid model for human-like bipedal walking is stated as an open question.
